title: Tokyo was once a different city with a different name: Edo.

claims.text: Before it was Tokyo, this city was called Edo
A map places it on Japan’s eastern coast, far from the old imperial capital
In 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu established his shogunate here, turning Edo into the seat of military government

evidence.excerpt: Tokugawa Ieyasu (born Matsudaira Takechiyo; January 31, 1543 – June 1, 1616) was a Japanese samurai, daimyo and the founder and first shogun of the Tokugawa shogunate of Japan, which ruled from 1603 until the Meiji Restoration in 1868

claims.text: The city grew through its waterways: boats carried goods, while bridges connected busy neighborhoods
Artists recorded these streets and canals in woodblock prints, making everyday Edo part of Japan’s visual memory
Panoramic views suggest how large the city became, though no single image can capture its whole past
Some traces remain in gardens such as Koishikawa Korakuen, where carefully shaped landscapes offer a quieter link to earlier eras
Nihonbashi was more than a crossing; it became a key starting point for roads across the country
